title: Room Games

source.quote: In Blemish, the player finds fault with others, criticizing their appearance, work, dress, etc.

setting: A different room, a different cast, every stop this week - a bar, a therapist's office, a corner store, a neighbor's porch. Same six-stage machinery underneath, dressed differently for sexual and Underworld games too (Rapo's come-on-then-rebuff, Let's You and Him Fight's manufactured rivalry) wherever they show up.
playAs: You, moving through all four rooms

L1.line: Did you see what Tanvi was wearing? And don't even get me started on Raj's new haircut...
cues: never a word about his own flaws
happening at a casual bar hangout
L1.question: Karan's running commentary on everyone's flaws, laughed off as teasing, at a casual bar hangout. Is this a Party game, a Consulting-Room game, an Underworld game, or a Good game?

options.feedback: Right - this is Blemish, played for laughs at a social gathering, exactly where Party games live: first-degree, time-structuring for a group, nobody involved is a client or a criminal.
Consulting-Room games (like Stupid or Wooden Leg) need a professional "helper" in the room - a therapist, doctor, teacher. There's no helper here, just a bar and some friends.
Underworld games (like Cops and Robbers) are about criminals and the people who chase them. Karan isn't dodging the law, he's dodging a mirror.
Good games still run a Switch and a Payoff, but the payoff benefits someone besides the player. Karan's running commentary benefits Karan - at everyone else's expense.

L1.lesson: GPP's game taxonomy sorts by social setting and who's in the room, not by how harmful the content feels: Party games run in casual social time-structuring, Consulting-Room games need a professional helper present, Underworld games involve crime and pursuit, and Good games keep the same structure but aim the payoff at someone other than the player.

L2.intro: Three more rooms this week: a counselor's office, a corner store, and a neighbor's porch.

beats.line: I've tried everything you've suggested, doctor, nothing works. I guess I'm just a hopeless case.
cues: fourth technique in four sessions, each one "doesn't work" within a week
slight brightening when he says "hopeless case"

options.text: Let's try one more approach - I have another idea.
options.outcome: Yusuf nods eagerly. Next week: "That one didn't work either, doctor."
options.lesson: Supplying idea number five keeps the Rescuer side of I'm Only Trying To Help You fully staffed - as long as there's always another technique coming, there's never a session where the pattern itself gets named.

options.text: I notice every technique I've offered has stopped working within a week. What do you make of that?
options.outcome: Yusuf shifts in his seat. "...I hadn't thought about it that way." First time the pattern itself is on the table instead of the content.
options.lesson: Naming the repeating shape - not the fourth failed technique, the pattern of techniques failing - is how a helper steps off the Rescuer role ITHY keeps offering.

options.text: Maybe you're not trying hard enough.
options.outcome: Yusuf's face falls. "I knew you'd eventually say that too." He gets his kick, right on schedule - and you've just confirmed his "I'm hopeless" belief for him.
options.lesson: This delivers the blame-the-Victim Switch he's fishing for, which actually completes his game's Payoff rather than interrupting it.

beats.line: ...Yeah, it's in my pocket. I mean, you were gonna find it anyway.
cues: left the tag half-ripped where anyone could see
more relieved than scared at getting caught
third time this month at this store

options.text: You're banned from this store, I'm calling your parents right now.
options.outcome: Deven shrugs, almost smiling. "Figured." The consequence lands and somehow still doesn't look like it touched anything underneath.
options.lesson: The real-world consequence is appropriate and necessary - and by itself, consequence is the Response stage of Cops and Robbers, not the exit from it; the thrill was never really about getting away with it.

options.text: You keep leaving the tags where we'll see them. What's actually going on?
options.outcome: Deven's smile drops. "I don't know. I guess I wanted someone to notice." First honest sentence of the conversation.
options.lesson: For a player who's set up to get caught, the game's real payoff is the getting-caught itself - asking about that, past the theft, is what starts to address the actual need underneath the game.

options.text: Wow, you must think this is hilarious.
options.outcome: "Yeah, maybe," Deven says, the small smile widening. Somehow the scolding is the best part of his day.
options.lesson: Persecuting delivers exactly the reaction a Cops-and-Robbers player is unconsciously angling for - the attention of being caught, dressed up as punishment.

beats.line: Oh, you're worrying about the exam again? Sit, sit - tell me what's actually confusing you, let's look at it together.
cues: fifth kid this month who's shown up on her porch unannounced
never brings it up unless asked, never takes credit afterward

options.text: You should charge for tutoring, you're basically running a business for free.
options.outcome: Mrs. Oyelaran laughs. "Maybe one day." Nothing changes - she wasn't doing this for payment, and the suggestion doesn't land anywhere.
options.lesson: Reasonable, practical advice aimed at a want she doesn't have - it misreads what's actually going on in the exchange.

options.text: Isn't it exhausting, having kids just show up like that?
options.outcome: "Some days," she admits, "but watching Deven's face when he gets it - that's the whole reason." She clearly isn't resentful, isn't collecting martyr points.
options.lesson: Looking for the hidden resentment assumes every helping pattern must secretly be I'm Only Trying To Help You - the tell that this one's different is that there's no Switch coming: ask her again next month, she'll still look like this.

options.text: This still runs on Formula G, doesn't it - so what makes it a GOOD game instead of a trap?
options.outcome: "Ha! Never thought of it that way. I suppose... because nobody ends up worse off. Not even me."
options.lesson: A Good game keeps the same structure - an ulterior transaction, something like a payoff - but the payoff benefits someone besides the player, or costs nobody anything real. Not every game is a trap; most of the famous ones just are.

echo.setting: Two days later. Karan starts up again at a different table, same opening line, new target.
echo.line: Okay but don't you think it's a LITTLE much, what she's wearing?
